listen_text: Section. Defining the Stages as the capital V subscript alpha s. In the source passage on chap , we defined well-orderings and the (von Neumann) ordinals. In this chapter, we will use these to characterise the hierarchy of sets itself. To do this, recall that in the source passage on sec , we defined the idea of successor and limit ordinals. We use these ideas in following definition: Definition. Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. capital V subscript the empty set is defined as the empty set. Then, capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha is defined as the power set of capital V subscript alpha for any ordinal, alpha. Then, capital V subscript alpha is defined as the union over gamma is less than alpha of capital V subscript gamma, when, alpha, is a limit ordinal. End display. End displayed expression. End definition. This will be a definition by transfinite recursion on the ordinals. In this regard, we should compare this with recursive definitions of functions on the natural numbers. Footnote. Cf. the definitions of addition, multiplication, and exponentiation in the source passage on sec . End footnote. As when dealing with natural numbers, one defines a base case and successor cases; but when dealing with ordinals, we also need to describe the behaviour of limit cases. This definition of the capital V subscript alpha s will be an important milestone. We have informally motivated our hierarchy of sets as forming sets by stages. The capital V subscript alpha s are, in effect, just those stages. Importantly, though, this is an internal characterisation of the stages. Rather than suggesting a possible model of the theory, we will have defined the stages within our set theory. End section.

listen_text: Section. Basic Properties of Stages. To bring out the foundational importance of the definition of the capital V subscript alpha s, we will present a few basic results about them. We start with a definition: Footnote. There's no standard terminology for “potent”; this is the name used by the cited work Button L Tone . End footnote. Definition. The set capital A is potent if and only if for every x, open scope, there exists y in capital A, x is a subset of y implies x belongs to capital A, close scope . End definition. Lemma. For each ordinal alpha : List. Next item. Each capital V subscript alpha is transitive. Next item. Each capital V subscript alpha is potent. Next item. If gamma belongs to alpha , then capital V subscript gamma belongs to capital V subscript alpha (and hence also capital V subscript gamma is a subset of capital V subscript alpha by the source passage on Valphatrans ) End list. End lemma. Proof. We prove this by a (simultaneous) transfinite induction. For induction, suppose that the source passage on Valphatrans — the source passage on Valphacum holds for each ordinal beta is less than alpha . The case of alpha equals the empty set is trivial. Suppose alpha equals the ordinal successor of beta . To show the source passage on Valphacum , if gamma belongs to alpha then capital V subscript gamma is a subset of capital V subscript beta by hypothesis, so capital V subscript gamma belongs to the power set of capital V subscript beta equals capital V subscript alpha . To show the source passage on Valphapotent , suppose capital A is a subset of capital B belongs to capital V subscript alpha that is, capital A is a subset of capital B is a subset of capital V subscript beta ; then capital A is a subset of capital V subscript beta so capital A belongs to capital V subscript alpha . To show the source passage on Valphatrans , note that if x belongs to capital A belongs to capital V subscript alpha we have capital A is a subset of capital V subscript beta , so x belongs to capital V subscript beta , so x is a subset of capital V subscript beta as capital V subscript beta is transitive by hypothesis, and so x belongs to capital V subscript alpha . Suppose alpha is a limit ordinal. To show the source passage on Valphacum , if gamma belongs to alpha then gamma belongs to the ordinal successor of gamma belongs to alpha , so that capital V subscript gamma belongs to capital V subscript the ordinal successor of gamma by assumption, hence capital V subscript gamma belongs to the union over beta belongs to alpha of capital V subscript beta equals capital V subscript alpha . To show the source passage on Valphatrans and the source passage on Valphapotent , just observe that a union of transitive (respectively, potent) sets is transitive (respectively, potent). End proof. Lemma. For each ordinal alpha , capital V subscript alpha does not belong to capital V subscript alpha . End lemma. Proof. By transfinite induction. Evidently capital V subscript the empty set does not belong to capital V subscript the empty set . If capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha belongs to capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha equals the power set of capital V subscript alpha , then capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha is a subset of capital V subscript alpha ; and since capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha by the source passage on Valphabasicprops , we have capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript alpha . Conversely: if capital V subscript alpha does not belong to capital V subscript alpha then capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha does not belong to capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha If alpha is a limit and capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript alpha equals the union over beta belongs to alpha of capital V subscript beta , then capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript beta for some beta belongs to alpha ; but then also capital V subscript beta belongs to capital V subscript alpha so that capital V subscript beta belongs to capital V subscript beta by the source passage on Valphabasicprops (twice). Conversely, if capital V subscript beta does not belong to capital V subscript beta for all beta belongs to alpha , then capital V subscript alpha does not belong to capital V subscript alpha . End proof. Corollary. For any ordinals alpha, then beta : alpha belongs to beta if and only if capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript beta End corollary. Proof. the source passage on Valphabasicprops gives one direction. Conversely, suppose capital V subscript alpha belongs to capital V subscript beta . Then alpha is not equal to beta by the source passage on Valphanotref ; and beta does not belong to alpha , for otherwise we would have capital V subscript beta belongs to capital V subscript alpha and hence capital V subscript beta belongs to capital V subscript beta by the source passage on Valphabasicprops (twice), contradicting the source passage on Valphanotref . So alpha belongs to beta by Trichotomy. End proof. All of this allows us to think of each capital V subscript alpha as the alpha indexed stage of the hierarchy. Here is why. Certainly our capital V subscript alpha s can be thought of as being formed in an iterative process, for our use of ordinals tracks the notion of iteration. Moreover, if one stage is formed before the other, that is, capital V subscript beta belongs to capital V subscript alpha , that is, beta belongs to alpha , then our process of formation is cumulative, since capital V subscript beta is a subset of capital V subscript alpha . Finally, we are indeed forming all possible collections of sets that were available at any earlier stage, since any successor stage capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha is the power-set of its predecessor capital V subscript alpha . In short: with set theory Z F minus , we are almost done, in articulating our vision of the cumulative-iterative hierarchy of sets. (Though, of course, we still need to justify Replacement.) End section.

listen_text: Section. Foundation. We are only almost done—and not quite finished—because nothing in set theory Z F minus guarantees that every set is in some capital V subscript alpha , that is, that every set is formed at some stage. Now, there is a fairly straightforward (mathematical) sense in which we don't care whether there are sets outside the hierarchy. (If there are any there, we can simply ignore them.) But we have motivated our concept of set with the thought that every set is formed at some stage (see Stages are key in the source passage on sec ). So we will want to preclude the possibility of sets which fall outside of the hierarchy. Accordingly, we must add a new axiom, which ensures that every set occurs somewhere in the hierarchy. Since the capital V subscript alpha s are our stages, we might simply consider adding the following as an axiom: Regularity. for every capital A, there exists alpha, capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha This would be a perfectly reasonable approach. However, for reasons that will be explained in the next section, we will instead adopt an alternative axiom: Axiom. Foundation. for every capital A not equal to the empty set, there exists capital B in capital A, capital A intersected with capital B equals the empty set . End axiom. With some effort, we can show (in set theory Z F minus ) that Foundation entails Regularity: Definition. For each set capital A , let: Displayed expression. Then, transitive closure of capital A equals the union over n is less than omega of closure stage n of capital A. End display. End displayed expression. We call transitive closure of capital A the transitive closure of capital A . End definition. Evidently capital A equals closure stage zero of capital A is a subset of transitive closure of capital A . End proof. Lemma. If capital A is a transitive set, then there is some alpha such that capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha . End lemma. Proof. End display. End displayed expression. Suppose capital D equals the empty set . So if x belongs to capital A , then there is some delta such that x is a subset of capital V subscript delta and, by the well-ordering of the ordinals, for every gamma in delta, x is not a subset of capital V subscript gamma ; hence delta belongs to alpha and so x belongs to capital V subscript alpha by the source passage on Valphabasicprops . By Foundation, there is some capital B belongs to capital D is a subset of capital A such that capital D intersected with capital B equals the empty set . End theorem. Proof. Fix capital A ; now capital A is a subset of the transitive closure of capital A by the source passage on subsetoftrcl , which is transitive. So there is some alpha such that capital A is a subset of the transitive closure of capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha by the lemma on Transitive Well Founded End proof. These results show that set theory Z F minus proves the conditional Foundation implies Regularity . In the source passage on zfminusregularityfoundation , we will show that set theory Z F minus proves Regularity implies Foundation . listen_text: Section. set theory Z and set theory Z F : A Milestone. With Foundation, we reach another important milestone. We have considered theories set theory Z minus and set theory Z F minus , which we said were certain theories “minus” a certain something. That certain something is Foundation. So: Definition. The theory set theory Z adds Foundation to set theory Z minus . So its axioms are Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, Foundation, and all instances of the Separation scheme. The theory set theory Z F adds Foundation to set theory Z F minus . Otherwise put, set theory Z F adds all instances of Replacement to set theory Z . End definition. Still, one question might have occurred to you. If Regularity is equivalent over set theory Z F minus to Foundation, and Regularity's justification is clear, why bother to go around the houses, and take Foundation as our basic axiom, rather than Regularity? Setting aside historical reasons (to do with who formulated what and when), the basic reason is that Foundation can be presented without employing the definition of the capital V subscript alpha s. That definition relied upon all of the work of the source passage on sec : we needed to prove Transfinite Recursion, to show that it was justified. But our proof of Transfinite Recursion employed Replacement. So, whilst Foundation and Regularity are equivalent modulo set theory Z F minus , they are not equivalent modulo set theory Z minus . Indeed, the matter is more drastic than this simple remark suggests. Though it goes well beyond this book's remit, it turns out that both set theory Z minus and set theory Z are too weak to define the capital V subscript alpha s. So, if you are working only in set theory Z , then Regularity (as we have formulated it) does not even make sense. This is why our official axiom is Foundation, rather than Regularity. From now on, we will work in set theory Z F (unless otherwise stated), without any further comment. End section.

Section. Rank. Now that we have defined the stages as the capital V subscript alpha apostrophe s , and we know that every set is a subset of some stage, we can define the rank of a set. Intuitively, the rank of capital A is the first moment at which capital A is formed. More precisely: Definition. For each set capital A , the rank of capital A is the least ordinal alpha such that capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha . End definition. Proposition. the rank of capital A exists, for any capital A . End proposition. Proof. Left as an exercise. End proof. Exercise. Prove the source passage on ranksexist . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. The well-ordering of ranks allows us to prove some important results: Proposition. For any ordinal alpha , capital V subscript alpha equals the set of x such that the rank of x belongs to alpha . End proposition. Proof. If the rank of x belongs to alpha then x is a subset of capital V subscript the rank of x belongs to capital V subscript alpha , so x belongs to capital V subscript alpha as capital V subscript alpha is potent (invoking the source passage on Valphabasicprops multiple times). Conversely, if x belongs to capital V subscript alpha then x is a subset of capital V subscript alpha , so the rank of x is less than or equal to alpha ; now a simple transfinite induction shows that x does not belong to capital V subscript alpha . Then the membership relation -Induction tells you the following: if phi is hereditary, every set is phi . To wrap up the discussion of ranks (for now), we'll prove a few claims which we have foreshadowed a few times. Proposition. the rank of capital A equals the strict supremum over x belongs to capital A of the rank of x . End proposition. Proof. Let alpha equals the strict supremum over x belongs to capital A of the rank of x . By the source passage on rankmemberslower , alpha is less than or equal to the rank of capital A . But if x belongs to capital A then the rank of x belongs to alpha , so that x belongs to capital V subscript alpha by the source passage on valphalowerrank , and hence capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha , that is, the rank of capital A is less than or equal to alpha .
